meta.label: Off-grid power systems
tradeoffLabels: cheapest price for the storage capacity you get
most charge cycles and the longest warranty before the battery needs replacing
meta.attribution: Covers real, purchasable off-grid power systems sold into the US market, from portable all-in-one power stations you can carry home and plug in the same day, to whole-home hybrid inverters that need a licensed installer and days of wiring, plus two routes that are not a product purchase: hiring a NABCEP-certified installer to design and build a custom system, and staying on the electric grid where it already reaches a property. Cost is scored only where a manufacturer publishes a fixed listed or sale price; several of the larger systems here (Sol-Ark, Victron's MultiPlus-II, MidNite Solar's components, EG4) are normally sold through installers or distributors at a price that varies by configuration, so no price is scored for them rather than guessed at. Battery cycle life and warranty length are pulled from each manufacturer's own product or warranty page. A safety record comes from the US Consumer Product Safety Commission's saferproducts.gov recall database, searched by brand name and dated 2026; where a recall exists it is named precisely, including when it applies to a different model from the same company than the one listed here, and where none was found the exact search term is given rather than treating silence as proof of safety. One real distinction runs through this roster: Generac's PWRcell, the battery brand many people already know from Generac's generators, states on its own product page that it 'is not an off-grid system' and needs the grid, solar or a generator to recharge, unlike Sol-Ark, EG4 or a Victron-based build, each designed to run independently of the grid. Suggest changes via Contribute.

products.name: Goal Zero Yeti PRO 4000
products.description: A 3,994Wh portable power station from Goal Zero, one of the oldest names in solar power stations. It is the most expensive unit per watt-hour in this roster, but carries the longest cycle rating of the portable options here.

economical.note: Goal Zero lists the Yeti PRO 4000 at $3,999.95 for 3993.6Wh of LiFePO4 capacity, close to $1.00 per watt-hour, the highest per-watt-hour price of any unit scored in this roster.

durability.note: Goal Zero states the Yeti PRO 4000 has a '4000+ cycle lifespan' with 'over 10 years of daily use' and a 5 year warranty.

accessibility.note: Goal Zero sells the Yeti PRO 4000 as a self-contained power station: no separate charge controller, inverter or installer is needed to start using it, only a wall outlet or solar panel to charge it.

safety.note: CPSC's saferproducts.gov database lists one Goal Zero recall, dated February 27, 2025, for the 'Solar Series Combiner Cable' accessory (model 98715), about 530 units, due to a fire hazard; it does not name the Yeti PRO 4000 power station itself.

links.label: CPSC: Goal Zero combiner cable recall

products.name: EcoFlow Delta Pro
products.description: A 3.6kWh portable power station from EcoFlow, expandable to 25kWh with extra battery packs, and one of the more affordable LFP units per watt-hour in this roster.

economical.note: EcoFlow lists the base DELTA Pro unit at $1,899 for 3.6kWh of expandable capacity, close to $0.53 per watt-hour, cheaper per watt-hour than the Goal Zero Yeti PRO 4000.

durability.note: EcoFlow's product page says the LFP battery 'supports up to 10 years' of daily use and lists '3000+ charging cycles,' backed by a '5-Year Warranty' made up of a 3-year standard term plus a 2-year extension available on app registration.

accessibility.note: The DELTA Pro is sold as a complete portable power station with no separate installer required, only a wall outlet, car charger or solar panel to charge it.

safety.note: CPSC's saferproducts.gov database lists one EcoFlow recall, dated October 9, 2025: the DELTA Max 2000 (model EFD310), about 25,030 units, recalled after six reports of the power station catching fire and over $850,000 in property damage. The recall names the Delta Max 2000, a different model from the Delta Pro listed here.

products.name: EcoFlow RIVER 3
products.description: A small 245Wh power station, the cheapest and smallest unit in this roster, big enough for phones, small appliances or a few hours of essentials rather than a whole home.

economical.note: EcoFlow lists the RIVER 3 at $229.00 for 245Wh of capacity, the lowest price of any unit in this roster.

durability.note: EcoFlow's product page rates the LiFePO4 battery at '3000 cycles to 80% capacity,' translating to about 10 years of everyday use before capacity drops to 80 percent, but does not state a warranty length on this page.

accessibility.note: At 245Wh, the RIVER 3 is small enough to carry and plug in immediately, with no installation of any kind.

products.name: Bluetti AC200MAX
products.description: A 2,048Wh power station from Bluetti, expandable to 8,192Wh with extra battery modules, sold at a mid-range price with the shortest stated warranty of the portable units here.

economical.note: Bluetti's own page lists the AC200MAX at a current sale price of $1,199.00, marked down from $1,699.00, for 2,048Wh, close to $0.59 per watt-hour at the sale price.

durability.note: Bluetti states the AC200MAX uses a 'LiFePO4 Battery with 3,500+ Life Cycles to 80%' and a '4-Year Hassle-Free Warranty,' the shortest warranty term of the portable power stations scored in this roster.

accessibility.note: The AC200MAX is a self-contained power station, expandable with extra battery modules but usable straight out of the box with no installer.

safety.note: CPSC's saferproducts.gov database returned no results when searched for 'Bluetti' in 2026.

products.name: Jackery Explorer 2000 Plus
products.description: A 2,042Wh LiFePO4 power station from Jackery, one of the best-known portable power brands and the one most people already recognize, even though its own product page gave little detail beyond capacity when checked here.

accessibility.note: Jackery's own product page names the Explorer 2000 Plus a 'Portable Power Station' with '2042Wh Capacity' and a LiFePO4 battery, sold as a complete unit rather than a component to be installed.

safety.note: CPSC's saferproducts.gov database returned no results when searched for 'Jackery' in 2026.

products.name: Anker SOLIX F3800
products.brand: large electronics brand's power station line
products.description: A 3,840Wh power station from Anker's SOLIX line, expandable to 53.8kWh with extra batteries, built around fast solar charging and a long-cycle battery Anker calls 'EV-grade.'

durability.note: Anker's tech specs list '3,000+ cycles' on 'LFP' chemistry described as 'EV-grade' with '10+ years of lifespan,' backed by a 5 year warranty.

safety.note: CPSC's saferproducts.gov database returned no results when searched for 'Anker SOLIX' in 2026. A broader search for 'Anker' alone returns an unrelated recall for a different company's baby bath seat, which is not connected to Anker or SOLIX.

products.name: Sol-Ark 15K-2P
products.description: A 15kW all-in-one hybrid inverter built for whole-home off-grid, grid-tied or battery-backup use, normally installed by a professional rather than bought off the shelf.

environment.note: Sol-Ark's own page for the 15K-2P describes 'Grid-Down Generation' that lets the system 'continue generating power independently from the grid during prolonged power outages or blackouts,' delivering 15,000W of AC output and 12,000W from batteries alone.

safety.note: CPSC's saferproducts.gov database returned no results when searched for 'Sol-Ark' in 2026, though a whole-home hybrid inverter this size is normally installed by a licensed electrician rather than sold as a standalone consumer product to begin with.

products.name: Victron Energy MultiPlus-II
products.description: An inverter/charger from the Dutch manufacturer Victron Energy, sold across a range of sizes from 3kVA to 15kVA and positioned for professional marine, vehicle and land-based off-grid installs rather than a plug-and-play consumer product.

durability.note: Victron's own MultiPlus-II page points to its 'industry-leading 5-year standard warranty and global repair service'.

accessibility.note: Victron markets the MultiPlus-II as 'suitable for professional marine, yachting, vehicle, and land-based off-grid systems,' language aimed at installers and system integrators rather than a buyer setting it up alone.

environment.note: Victron says the MultiPlus-II uses 'a smart adaptive algorithm that extends battery life' during charging, and switches to inverter power in under 20 milliseconds when grid or generator power is disconnected.

safety.note: CPSC's saferproducts.gov database returned no results when searched for 'Victron' in 2026.

products.name: Generac PWRcell 2
products.description: A home battery system from Generac, the brand most US homeowners already know from fuel generators. Generac's own page for PWRcell 2 states plainly that it is not built to run a home independent of the grid.

durability.note: Generac's PWRcell 2 page states the system carries a '10 years' warranty on its components, and offers 9 to 18kWh per battery cabinet, up to 36kWh with two cabinets stacked.

safety.note: CPSC's saferproducts.gov database returned no results for 'PWRcell' specifically in 2026; a broader search for 'Generac' does return active recalls for other Generac product lines, such as electric-start pressure washers, which shows the database does cover the brand and the absence for PWRcell is not simply an unindexed name.

products.name: MidNite Solar Classic MPPT
products.description: An MPPT charge controller, one component of a self-built off-grid system rather than a complete unit, sold to be paired with a separate inverter and battery bank chosen by the buyer.

accessibility.note: MidNite markets the Classic as 'NORTH AMERICA'S MOST SOPHISTICATED MPPT CHARGE CONTROLLER,' with Ethernet, USB and RS232 monitoring and '20 megs of data logging,' a component for someone assembling their own system rather than a plug-and-play unit.

safety.note: CPSC's saferproducts.gov database returned no results when searched for 'MidNite' in 2026.

products.name: EG4 6000XP
products.description: A 6kW all-in-one off-grid inverter popular in the DIY off-grid community, taking up to 8kW of solar input and able to run split-phase on its own or paired with grid or generator input.

environment.note: EG4's own product page calls the 6000XP an 'All-In-One Off-Grid Inverter' and describes it as 'a 48V split-phase inverter/charger, providing powerful and efficient off-grid energy solutions', with 8kW of PV input and 6kW of output.

safety.note: CPSC's saferproducts.gov database returned no results when searched for 'EG4' in 2026.

products.name: Hire a NABCEP-certified installer
products.description: Paying a certified professional to design, size and install a custom off-grid system rather than choosing a product yourself. NABCEP is the credentialing body most of the industry recognizes for this work.

accessibility.note: NABCEP, a nonprofit certification body founded in 2002, says it gives consumers 'a way to hold unethical installers accountable' through an enforceable Code of Ethics, and lists certified professionals in a public directory, so a buyer with no technical background can find and vet an installer rather than needing to design a system alone.

products.name: Staying on the electric grid
products.description: Not buying an off-grid system at all: for a property the electric grid already reaches, staying connected is usually the cheapest way to keep the lights on, and needs nothing installed.

economical.note: University of Wyoming Extension's comparison of rural power options found utility line extension typically costs about $20,000 a mile to build new, but also lists a utility fixed charge above $265 a year as one signal that switching away from an existing connection pays off, which by the same logic means a property already paying less than that to stay connected is hard to beat on cost.

accessibility.note: There is nothing to buy, size or install: a property already wired to the grid keeps its power by doing nothing.
